The Trigonometric Functions
section.paragraph: Let $$P\left( {x,y} \right)$$ be a point on the unit circle such that the radius $$\overline{OP}$$ forms an angle of $$\theta$$ radians with respect to the positive $$x$$ -axis (see Figure 7).

From P, a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis. The length of the perpendicular is labeled y. The distance between the origin and where the perpendicular touches the x axis is labeled x. figure.caption: $$P$$ is a point on the unit circle with coordinates $$x = \cos\theta$$ and $$y = \sin\theta$$ .

section.paragraph: We define the sine of the angle $$\theta$$ , written $$\sin\theta$$ , to be the $$y$$ -coordinate of $$P$$ . Similarly, the cosine of the angle $$\theta$$ , written $$\cos\theta$$ , is defined to be the $$x$$ -coordinate of $$P$$ . The other trigonometric functions, tangent, cosecant, secant, and cotangent of $$\theta$$ —written $$\tan\theta$$ , $$\csc\theta$$ , $$\sec\theta$$ , and $$\cot\theta$$ , respectively—are defined in terms of the sine and cosine functions.

section.paragraph: As you work with trigonometric functions, it will be helpful to remember the values of the sine, cosine, and tangent of some important angles, such as $$\theta = 0,\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{2}$$ , and so on. These values may be found by using elementary geometry and algebra.
For example, if $$\theta = 0$$ , then the point $$P$$ has coordinates $$(1,0)$$ (see Figure 8a), and we see that
$$\sin 0 = y = 0 \cos 0 = x = 1 \tan 0 = \frac{y}{x} = 0$$

section.paragraph: The next example illustrates how we find the trigonometric functions of an angle.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find the sine, cosine, and tangent of $$\frac{5\pi}{4}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: We first determine the reference angle for the given angle. As is indicated in Figure 11, the reference angle is $$\frac{5\pi}{4} - \pi = \frac{\pi}{4}$$ , or $$45^{{^\circ}}$$ . Since $$\sin 45^{{^\circ}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$$ and the sine is negative in Quadrant III, we conclude that $$\sin\frac{5\pi}{4} = \frac{- \sqrt{2}}{2}$$ . Similarly, since $$\cos 45^{{^\circ}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$$ and the cosine is negative in Quadrant III, we conclude that $$\cos\frac{5\pi}{4} = \frac{- \sqrt{2}}{2}$$ . Finally, since $$\tan 45^{{^\circ}} = 1$$ and the tangent is positive in Quadrant III, we conclude that $$\tan\frac{5\pi}{4} = 1$$ .

section.paragraph: Therefore,
$$\sin\left( {\theta + 2\pi} \right) = \sin\theta {and} \cos\left( {\theta + 2\pi} \right) = \cos\theta$$
and
$$\sin\left( {\theta + 2n\pi} \right) = \sin\theta {and} \cos\left( {\theta + 2n\pi} \right) = \cos\theta$$
for every real number $$\theta$$ and every integer $$n$$ , and we say that the sine and cosine functions are periodic with period $$2\pi$$ .

section.paragraph: To sketch the graph of $$y = \tan x$$ , we first note that $$\tan x = \left( {\sin x} \right) \slash \left( {\cos x} \right)$$ . So $$\tan x$$ is not defined when $$\cos x = 0$$ , that is, when $$x = \frac{\pi}{2} \pm n\pi\left( {n = 0,1,2,3,\ldots} \right)$$ . The function is defined at all other points, so the domain of the tangent function is the set of all real numbers with the exception of the points just noted. Next, we can show that the vertical lines with equation $$x = \frac{\pi}{2} \pm n\pi\left( {n = 0,1,2,3,\ldots} \right)$$ are vertical asymptotes of the graph of $$f(x) = \tan x$$ . For example, since we can readily verify with the help of a calculator that
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow{({\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\tan x = \infty$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow{({\pi \slash 2})}^{+}}\tan x = - \infty$$

we conclude that $$x = \frac{\pi}{2}$$ is a vertical asymptote of the graph of $$y = \tan x$$ . Finally, using Table 2, we sketch the graph of $$y = \tan x$$ (Figure 16). Observe that the tangent function is periodic with period $$\pi$$ . It follows that
$$\tan\left( {x + n\pi} \right) = \tan x$$
whenever $$n$$ is an integer.

section.paragraph: Next, let’s compare the graphs of $$y = \cos 2x$$ and $$y = \cos\left( {x \slash 2} \right)$$ with the graph of $$y = \cos x$$ (see Figure 18a–b). Notice here that the factor of $$2$$ has the effect of “speeding up” the graph of the cosine: The period is decreased from $$2\pi$$ to $$\pi$$ . In contrast, the factor of $$\frac{1}{2}$$ has the effect of “slowing down” the graph of the cosine: The period is increased from $$2\pi$$ to $$4\pi$$ . In general, the period of both $$y = \sin Bx$$ and $$y = \cos Bx$$ is $$2\pi \slash |B|$$ if $$B \neq 0$$ .

note.paragraph: From the graphs, we see that at time $$t = 0$$ , the predator population stands at $$1000$$ owls. As it increases, the prey population decreases from $$24,000$$ mice at that instant of time. Eventually, this decrease in the food supply causes the predator population to decrease, which in turn causes an increase in the prey population. But as the prey population increases, resulting in an increase in food supply, the predator population once again increases. The cycle is complete and starts all over again.

section.heading: Trigonometric Identities
section.paragraph: Equations that express the relationships between trigonometric functions, such as
$$\sin\left( {- \theta} \right) = - \sin\theta$$
and
$$\cos\left( {- \theta} \right) = \cos\theta$$

are called trigonometric identities . Some other important trigonometric identities are listed in Table 3. Each identity holds true for every value of $$\theta$$ in the common domain of the specified functions. The proofs of these identities may be found in any elementary trigonometry book.
